references.text: Jesus expresses his sorrow over Jerusalem and its repeated rejection of God's messengers: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you! How often I have wanted to gather your children" ([ref:Luk 13:34-35|Luke 13:34-35]). This lament shows the same deep sorrow over the city as in Luke 19:41.

The prophet Jeremiah weeps for his people and their destruction: "Over my people's crushed daughter, I am crushed" ([ref:Jer 8:21-22|Jeremiah 8:21-22]). Jesus' weeping over Jerusalem parallels Jeremiah's sorrow as "the weeping prophet."

Jeremiah's deep sorrow is expressed: "Oh that my head were a spring of water and my eyes a fountain of tears! Then I would weep day and night for the slain among my people" ([ref:Jer 9:1|Jeremiah 9:1]). Jesus shows similar prophetic grief over Jerusalem's coming fate.

David weeps as he flees from Jerusalem up the Mount of Olives: "David went up weeping by the road to the Mount of Olives" ([ref:2 Sam 15:30|2 Samuel 15:30]). Jesus also weeps over Jerusalem right at the Mount of Olives, creating a strong typological parallel between David and Jesus.

Jesus' weeping in verse 41 is immediately followed by the prophecy of Jerusalem's destruction: "Days will come upon you when your enemies will build an embankment around you" ([ref:Luk 19:43-44|Luke 19:43-44]). This gives the reason for his tears – he sees the city's coming downfall.

Isaiah prophesies about Jerusalem's siege: "Woe to Ariel, Ariel, the city where David encamped!" ([ref:Jes 29:1-4|Isaiah 29:1-4]). The prophecy of the siege and destruction of Jerusalem is the background for Jesus' sorrow.

"Jesus wept" ([ref:Joh 11:35|John 11:35]). At Lazarus' tomb, Jesus shows the same deep human compassion and sorrow as when he weeps over Jerusalem. In both places, Jesus' full humanity and his love are revealed.

Moses laments that Israel's people lack understanding and insight: "For they are a people without sense, there is no discernment in them. If only they were wise!" ([ref:5 Mos 32:28-29|Deuteronomy 32:28-29]). Jesus' weeping is precisely because Jerusalem did not know its time of visitation (v. 44).

God's heart turns within him over the fate of his people: "My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender" ([ref:Hos 11:8|Hosea 11:8]). Jesus' weeping over Jerusalem reflects God's own deep pain at having to judge his people.
